transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

Probably not. A noticeable buzz or hum from an induction hob on maximum power is usually normal, particularly with a large, heavy or multi-layer stockpot. The magnetic layers in the base can vibrate slightly in the induction field, and some pans amplify that into a loud hum. 1. Try the same zone with another flat, magnetic pan on high. If the noise is only with the stockpot, the pan is resonating rather than the hob failing.
2. Make sure the stockpot base is clean, dry and sitting flat on the glass. A warped or slightly domed base can be much noisier.
3. Reduce from maximum by one or two power levels. If the hum drops markedly but heating remains normal, that also fits normal induction behaviour. It becomes a fault concern if there is loud cracking, a burning or hot-plastic smell, sparking, an error display, or the hob cuts out. In any of those cases, stop using it and isolate it at the hob switch; it would need an engineer. If it only hums with that pot on high and otherwise cooks normally, it is not a sign that it is about to break.

I tried a few things. My heavy cast iron pot is quiet on the same zone, but the new stockpot and a cheap frying pan are both noisy. It's much quieter at power level 6 and below. The stockpot has a sandwich base that might be slightly smaller than the ring. There's sometimes a slight crackle but no burning smell, no error codes, and it hasn't cut out.

This does not sound like the hob is about to fail. The quiet cast-iron pot on the same zone is the key result: it shows the zone is operating normally. The new sandwich-base stockpot and cheaper frying pan are likely resonating at the high-power switching frequency; a base that is smaller than the marked cooking zone can make that more noticeable. The slight crackle can also be normal with induction cookware, provided it is only a light intermittent sound and there is no smell, sparking, display error or loss of heating. The fact it becomes much quieter at level 6 and below strongly supports cookware noise rather than a hob fault. Practical answer: use that stockpot on a better-matched zone if available, keep it centred with a clean dry base, and use level 6–8 once the contents are boiling. There is no part to replace on the evidence so far. Stop using the hob and arrange an engineer if the crackle becomes a sharp electrical snapping sound, you see sparks, smell burning/hot plastic, get an error code, or the hob starts cutting out with pans that are normally quiet.

candidates: Normal induction-pan vibration/resonance at high power (high)
Stockpot base is slightly uneven or made from layered material that resonates (medium)
Induction power module or cooling system fault (low)

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
